title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: one Upanishad sentence says what the self is not, and then what it is, and Ramanuja builds on holding both halves

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened Vaishnava theology with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, the book that states the other view first. Whose side did you say out loud, fairly? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `TODAY: WITHOUT, AND WITH.`

segments.voice: Free from evil. Free from old age. Free from death, from grief, from hunger, from thirst. That's how the Chandogya Upanishad begins describing the self it wants us to seek. A long run of withouts. So far, it sounds like the self is defined by what it isn't. And then, in the same breath, the sentence turns. Whose desires are real. Whose resolves come true. Suddenly there's someone there: someone who wants, and whose wanting is never empty. One sentence, two halves, a no and a yes. Some readers lean on the first half. Ramanuja says you have to keep both, and today we watch him do it.
screen: `FREE FROM EVIL, AGE, DEATH, GRIEF.` → `THEN: WHOSE DESIRES ARE REAL.` → `A NO AND A YES.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads sometimes call Brahman nirguna, without qualities. Other passages pile qualities on: all-knowing, all-powerful, the source of joy. How do you read a text that seems to say both? Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, read the withouts as the highest truth, and the qualities as true from where we stand, a lower vantage. Ramanuja, in the Sri Bhashya, reads it another way. Without qualities, he says, means without bad qualities. No evil, no decay, no limit, no lack. And the qualities the texts praise, knowledge, power, compassion, beauty, are fully real in Brahman. So the no and the yes aren't two levels. They're one portrait, drawn from both sides: everything wrong ruled out, everything good affirmed. Sri Vaishnava teachers have a phrase for that: Brahman as an ocean of auspicious qualities. That's why the Chandogya sentence matters so much to him. It shows the pattern inside a single line: free from evil, and whose desires are real. Neither half cancels the other. For Ramanuja, this has a human side. A God with every good quality and no flaw is someone you can bring a grief to, sing a song to, as the Alvars did. Ramanuja's theology and the Alvars' devotion meet right here. Both schools argue carefully from the same Upanishads, and both have their reasons; we're not here to rank them, only to hear Ramanuja clearly.
screen: `NIRGUNA: WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `WITHOUT BAD QUALITIES.` · `AN OCEAN OF GOOD QUALITIES.` · `SOMEONE YOU CAN TALK TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a no and a yes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you love. First, the withouts. Let go, for a moment, of every complaint you have about them: what they forgot, what annoys you. Just set those down. A few breaths. Then the yes. Name, quietly, the good that's really in them: their patience, their laugh, the way they show up. Stay with both, the faults set down and the good held up. If you pray, you can turn the same no and yes toward the name you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vaishnava theology. Today, without qualities read as without bad qualities, and an ocean of good ones: a no and a yes in one portrait. Today's word.
Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). Today, when you describe someone, add one real good quality after any complaint. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas study the Sri Bhashya's reading of nirguna with a teacher, and in worship they praise Vishnu and Lakshmi through their qualities, in hymns, names and stotras that list the Lord's good qualities one by one.

match.prompt: a no and a yes: tap the pairs.

myth: for Ramanuja, Brahman has no qualities at all
he reads without qualities as without bad ones, and every good quality as real.
one Chandogya sentence holds both withouts and withs
free from evil, age and death, and whose desires are real.
Advaita and Ramanuja read the same Upanishads differently
both read the same texts carefully, each with its own reasons.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja. one Upanishad says Brahman is without qualities, another praises Brahman's knowledge and power. how do you read them together?
options: without qualities means without bad qualities; the good ones are real.
only the qualities are real; ignore the withouts.
the texts contradict each other; pick one.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads the no and the yes as one portrait: every fault ruled out, every good quality affirmed.

original.note: Sanskrit: without qualities. Ramanuja reads it as without bad qualities.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirguna means God has no qualities.
what it means: for Ramanuja, it means no bad qualities, while every good quality is real.
what a scholar hears: the Chandogya 8.1.5 and 8.7.1 pattern, apahatapapma and satyakama, read as Brahman's two marks: free of all faults, full of auspicious qualities.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1 (the self free from evil, age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, whose desires and resolves are real)
Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya, on nirguna and saguna texts (e.g. under 1.1.1 and 3.2)

notes: Chandogya 8.7.1 (and 8.1.5) is paraphrased; Max Müller's 1879 SBE translation exists but the exact wording wasn't certain, so nothing is quoted.
Advaita's reading is summarized in one sentence (the qualities true from a lower vantage, vyavaharika); an Advaita reader should confirm it is fair.
Where exactly in the Sri Bhashya Ramanuja makes the 'without bad qualities' argument most clearly should be checked; references given loosely.
'Ocean of auspicious qualities' (kalyana-guna-akara) is a standard Sri Vaishnava phrase; confirm wording.
Editor: a myth reveal that referred to 'the script' was rewritten to speak of the two schools themselves; no other change.
